aiOverview.content: An orbit is a regular, repeating gravitational path of an object, such as a planet, moon, or satellite, around a central body. It is a curved trajectory—typically elliptical—governed by the balance between an object’s velocity and the force of gravity. Key types include low Earth orbit (LEO), geostationary orbit (GEO), and polar orbit. Key Characteristics and Components Definition: The path of an object in space around another, or a set of points in a dynamical system. Shape: Most orbits are elliptical (oval), though they can be perfectly circular or parabolic. Components: Key elements include the central body, the orbiting object (satellite), and the force of gravity. Speed: Objects must move at a specific velocity, known as orbital velocity, to maintain their path without falling back or flying away. Perigee/Periapsis: The point in an orbit closest to the body being orbited. Apogee/Apoapsis: The point in an orbit farthest from the body being orbited. Types of Orbits Low Earth Orbit (LEO): Close to Earth (160 to 2,000 km altitude), typically used for space stations and satellites. Geostationary Orbit (GEO): A circular orbit 35,786 km above Earth's equator, allowing satellites to stay over the same spot. Polar Orbit: An orbit that passes over or near both poles. Sun-Synchronous Orbit: A nearly polar orbit that passes over any given spot on Earth's surface at the same local solar time. How Orbit is Calculated & Key EquationsOrbits are calculated using celestial mechanics, often relying on Newton's law of universal gravitation and Kepler's laws of planetary motion. Gravity Equation: 𝐹=𝐺𝑚1𝑚2𝑟2 (Force equals gravitational constant times the two masses divided by the distance squared). Orbital Velocity: 𝑣=𝐺𝑀𝑟 (Velocity equals the square root of the gravitational constant times the central mass divided by the radius). History of the Concept Ancient Views: Early astronomers believed in geocentric models where everything orbited the Earth. Copernican Revolution: Nicolaus Copernicus proposed a heliocentric (sun-centered) model. Kepler and Newton: Johannes Kepler determined that orbits were elliptical (not perfectly circular), and Isaac Newton later developed the physical laws explaining why objects orbit. Space Age: In 1962, John Glenn became the first American to enter Earth orbit. Common Uses Satellites: Telecommunications, navigation (GPS), weather monitoring, and scientific research. Space Exploration: International Space Station (ISS), lunar missions. Physics: In atomic models, electrons orbit the nucleus.

references.title: What is an Orbit in Physics? Definition: An orbit is the curved path followed by an object under the influence of gravity as it moves around a larger body, such as a planet around the Sun or a satellite around Earth. Explanation: Orbits occur because of a balance between forward motion and gravitational pull: • Gravity pulls the object inward. • Forward velocity keeps it moving sideways. • The result is continuous free fall around the central body, instead of crashing into it. Types of Orbits: • Circular orbit → constant distance from centre. • Elliptical orbit → varying distance, with closest point = perihelion/perigee and farthest = aphelion/apogee. • Geostationary orbit → satellite appears fixed over one spot on Earth (24-hour period). Imagine: Think of swinging a stone tied to a string. The string pulls the stone inward (like gravity), while the stone’s speed keeps it moving in a circle, that’s how orbits work. In simple terms: An orbit is the path an object takes when it keeps “falling around” another object due to gravity. Formula (Orbital Velocity): v = √(GM/R) Where: • G = gravitational constant • M = mass of central body • R = distance
